title: NorthPeak x Redwood - Dedicated autoscaling bounds (min floor / max cap) + audit logs
next_steps: Redwood to send a one-pager on Dedicated autoscaling bounds semantics (hard max, min behavior during drains/maintenance) and the scaling event audit trail fields.
NorthPeak to share a week of traffic patterns (QPS/token rate by hour) and any known event calendar (marketing launches / batch jobs).
Schedule a 60-min sizing + pilot scoping session focused on min/max defaults, cooldowns, and expected throttling behavior at max.
Redwood to provide security materials relevant to audit logging (config change history, scaling decision logs, retention/export options) and confirm SOC 2 details.
transcript:
Meeting title: NorthPeak x Redwood - Dedicated autoscaling bounds (min floor / max cap) + audit logs
Recorded: 2025-11-19 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 47 minutes

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood) 
- Hyejin Park (Redwood)
- Dylan Hart (NorthPeak) 
- Priya Desai (NorthPeak)
- Evan Cho (NorthPeak)
- Marta Klein (NorthPeak)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
NorthPeak is evaluating Redwood Dedicated and is specifically looking for strict spend controls during traffic anomalies (hard maximum capacity cap) while still guaranteeing a baseline of performance (minimum capacity floor). The team asked detailed questions about how Redwood enforces min/max bounds, how scale decisions are made (reactive vs predictive), and what audit logs are available for both config changes and scaling events. Redwood clarified that max should be enforced as a hard clamp, discussed best-effort behavior for min during maintenance/drains, and outlined audit trail visibility in Console plus export options. NorthPeak wants guidance/warnings for the scenario where max is set too low and throttling occurs.

Topics
- Dedicated pool autoscaling config (min/max replicas / min/max GPUs)
- Burst-to-max, cooldowns, and scale-rate limits
- Predictive pre-scale signals vs reactive scaling
- Fleet constraints and what happens if max is hit (throttling/degradation)
- Audit logging: who changed what, scaling reason codes, retention/export
- Pilot success criteria and next steps

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood: send bounds semantics + audit log field list
- NorthPeak: share traffic patterns + known peak events
- Redwood/NorthPeak: schedule sizing workshop

Questions (auto-generated)
- Is max a hard cap even if p95 latency is bad?
- What happens to min during maintenance/drains or regional supply issues?
- Can we see “why did it scale” and “who changed the max” in audit logs?
- How does forecasting work and what happens if the prediction is wrong?

---
Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, cool. I think folks are joining. Dylan, Priya, Evan, Marta — good to see you. I’m Markus, I run solutions engineering for Dedicated. Hyejin is here as well, she’s been deep in the autoscaling and sizing side.

[00:18] Dylan Hart: Hey Markus. Thanks for making time.

[00:21] Hyejin Park: Hi everyone.

[00:23] Markus Klein: The agenda we had was basically: you all asked specifically about min and max bounds for Dedicated pools, and also auditability for scaling events and config changes. We can go as deep as you want. Maybe, Dylan, quick framing from your side? What’s driving the “hard cap” requirement.

[00:41] Dylan Hart: Yeah. So we have… we run an internal assistant plus a customer-facing chat feature. It’s spiky. The scary part is like one bad deploy or a partner sending us, you know, 10x traffic, and then suddenly our GPU bill is… not bounded. We’ve been burned before.

[00:59] Evan Cho: And FinOps angle: we do need an upper bound that’s enforceable. Like not “best effort,” not “we’ll try.” It needs to be a contractable limit.

[01:08] Markus Klein: Makes sense. And then on the flip side you want a floor, right.

[01:11] Priya Desai: Yeah. If we overreactively scale down at night and then morning ramp hits, we get queueing and p95 goes to the moon. So we want a min baseline that’s not fighting us.

[01:23] Markus Klein: Got it. And you’re thinking Redwood Dedicated, not Hosted, because of predictable throughput and isolation?

[01:30] Priya Desai: Exactly. Also we have some data residency constraints for one product line. Not fully on-prem, but we need VPC controls.

[01:38] Marta Klein: And audit logs. We need to show in an audit who changed autoscaling settings, and then separately, why the system scaled. If it scaled up, what signal drove that. And retention/export.

[01:50] Markus Klein: Yep, understood.

[01:52] Hyejin Park: Can I ask, what are you using today? Are you on EKS with vLLM, or…?

[01:56] Priya Desai: Yeah. EKS. vLLM. We do our own autoscaling with KEDA, it’s mostly queue depth. It’s… fine until it isn’t. Also we have multiple models and it’s messy.

[02:09] Markus Klein: Okay.

[02:10] Evan Cho: And it’s not “Dedicated” from a provider, it’s just our nodes. So when we hit a spike it can start scaling node groups. That’s where we got surprised — the max nodes was set too high and we didn’t notice.

[02:23] Markus Klein: Yep. So we’ve been building exactly for that: explicit per-pool min and max bounds. Let me start with semantics, then Hyejin can talk about operational behavior.

[02:34] Markus Klein: For Redwood Dedicated, you have a Dedicated pool, think of it as a set of replicas backing a model route. In config, you can specify a minimum and maximum capacity — depending on the hardware mode it’s either min/max replicas or min/max GPUs, but functionally it’s a bound on the number of serving workers.

[02:52] Dylan Hart: We want max to be hard. Like “cannot go above,” even if latency is terrible.

[02:58] Markus Klein: Yes. The design is a hard clamp. Desired capacity is computed by autoscaler, then we clamp within [min, max]. If you are at max and demand exceeds, you’ll see throttling/queueing rather than scaling past your max.

[03:14] Evan Cho: That’s good.

[03:15] Priya Desai: But then how do we avoid setting max too low and shooting ourselves.

[03:20] Hyejin Park: That’s a key part. We usually pair hard max with two things: (1) console warnings / sizing guidance and (2) optional burst behavior within the cap plus cool downs.

[03:33] Hyejin Park: So like you can set min=20, max=40. If you normally run at 20 but you have lunch peaks, you can allow burst to 40 quickly, but you can also set a scale-up rate limit so it doesn’t jump from 20 to 40 in one 30-second loop unless signals are very strong.

[03:52] Priya Desai: When you say “signals,” what are you using? GPU util? Queue? Latency?

[03:58] Hyejin Park: We blend reactive signals like queue depth and throughput and p95 latency, plus GPU utilization and request throttles. Then there’s an option to incorporate predictive signals — basically short horizon forecast on token rate / QPS.

[04:14] Dylan Hart: We asked about forecasting because reactive is too slow. The ramp time kills us.

[04:20] Hyejin Park: Right. The predictive system basically says “in 5 minutes you’re going to need 30, not 20,” so we start scaling early, but there’s confidence gating. If forecast confidence is low, we fall back to reactive.

[04:34] Evan Cho: But doesn’t that risk overprovisioning and cost.

[04:37] Markus Klein: That’s where max is your safety belt. Predictive can only act within bounds. And we also do safety margins that are tied to confidence, so low confidence means smaller pre-scale.

[04:52] Marta Klein: I want to make sure we can see that. If it scaled up because “forecast,” we need a log that says that.

[04:58] Markus Klein: Yes. There’s a scaling decision log entry per actuation. It includes inputs and a reason code. Things like “queue_depth_high,” “latency_slo_risk,” “forecast_up,” and also “clamped_to_max” if it wanted higher but hit your cap.

[05:15] Priya Desai: Nice. And min — is min also hard?

[05:18] Markus Klein: Min is… mostly hard, but there are operational exceptions. Hyejin, want to describe maintenance/drains.

[05:25] Hyejin Park: Yeah. If we’re doing a maintenance drain or a hardware evacuation, we try to keep you at or above min in aggregate. But there are cases like region capacity shortage or a node failure where you might temporarily go below min.

[05:40] Dylan Hart: So it’s best effort.

[05:42] Hyejin Park: It’s “best effort min” in those exceptional cases. In normal scaling behavior, we do not scale down below min.

[05:50] Evan Cho: For contract language, can we say max is hard, min is target/best-effort.

[05:56] Markus Klein: That’s typically how we position it. Max is a strict spend control. Min is a performance floor, but subject to real-world capacity events.

[06:05] Marta Klein: I’m going to be annoying: does your audit log capture min being violated due to maintenance.

[06:10] Markus Klein: Not annoying. Yes, we log events that would explain that. There are separate fleet events, and for scaling we’d show “applied_replicas < min” with a reason like “capacity_unavailable” or “drain_in_progress.”

[06:25] Marta Klein: And also config changes, like who changed max from 40 to 20.

[06:30] Markus Klein: That’s a separate audit stream: configuration changes. It captures actor, time, old value, new value, and the API client or console user.

[06:41] Marta Klein: And can we export to SIEM.

[06:44] Markus Klein: We have export options. The common one is webhook-based export and then customers feed to Splunk or Sentinel. We can confirm specifics in security review.

[06:54] Marta Klein: Ok.

[06:56] Priya Desai: Back to scaling. How fast can it scale? Like from 20 to 40, what’s the typical time.

[07:03] Hyejin Park: In Dedicated, if the capacity is already reserved in your pool, scale is relatively fast — you’re mostly starting replicas and warming. It’s on the order of a couple minutes, sometimes faster. If it requires provisioning new GPUs, that’s longer, but in Dedicated we try to keep it within your reserved pool.

[07:22] Dylan Hart: We’re not trying to do “spot” style. It’s reserved.

[07:24] Hyejin Park: Exactly.

[07:26] Evan Cho: Wait, so is “max” within what we pay for, or could it allocate beyond.

[07:31] Markus Klein: In Dedicated, max is within your committed reserved capacity if you buy that way. If you have a burst add-on, that’s an explicit configuration. But regardless, the max bound is the enforcement point: we won’t exceed max replicas.

[07:47] Evan Cho: Okay.

[07:48] Priya Desai: What about like multi-region. We’re considering active-active.

[07:52] Markus Klein: Multi-region Dedicated can be done, but bounds semantics can differ — per-region pool vs global. For most customers, bounds are per pool per region. That avoids ambiguous “40 total across two regions” behavior.

[08:07] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[08:10] Markus Klein: Let me ask: what are your success criteria for pilot? That helps us pick initial min/max.

[08:16] Dylan Hart: For customer chat, we need p95 under 900ms end-to-end. For internal assistant it’s looser.

[08:23] Priya Desai: Also we need no surprise spend. We can tolerate throttling, but it needs to be visible and alertable.

[08:31] Evan Cho: And we want to understand our unit cost per 1k tokens. But that’s secondary.

[08:38] Markus Klein: Great. On throttling visibility: you’ll see rate-limit/throttle metrics and also in the scaling history you’ll see “hit max” and “clamped.”

[08:49] Priya Desai: Is there a way to warn in console when you set max too low.

[08:54] Hyejin Park: We’re adding warnings like “Your configured max is below observed steady-state demand” and “At current traffic, you will likely see throttling.” It’s not perfect, but it uses historical token rate and headroom.

[09:10] Marta Klein: Is that logged too? The warnings.

[09:12] Markus Klein: The warnings are mostly UI, but the underlying signals are metrics. The key audit requirements usually focus on changes and scaling events.

[09:22] Dylan Hart: We also need to know: if something tries to scale beyond max, it should not do it anyway, even if Redwood’s SRE tries.

[09:30] Markus Klein: The system respects your configured max. Operationally, there are break-glass procedures for emergencies, but that’s not something we’d do without customer approval. And for compliance, break-glass access is audited.

[09:44] Marta Klein: Good answer.

[09:46] Priya Desai: Can you talk more about scale-down? Because that’s where we got burned. Like it scales down and then warm-up cost, and we miss the ramp.

[09:56] Hyejin Park: Scale-down is controlled by cooldowns and hysteresis. We avoid oscillation by requiring sustained low demand before reducing. And min gives you a base. For example, if min=20, we’ll never go below 20 just because traffic dipped for 5 minutes.

[10:12] Priya Desai: But what about going from 40 back to 20 after a burst.

[10:17] Hyejin Park: That’s the cooldown. You can set “stay at elevated capacity for N minutes” after scaling up. That reduces flapping.

[10:24] Dylan Hart: We want that.

[10:26] Evan Cho: But it means higher spend.

[10:28] Dylan Hart: Predictable spend, Evan.

[10:30] Evan Cho: (laughs) bounded spend.

[10:33] Markus Klein: Yeah, it’s a trade.

[10:36] Marta Klein: On audit logs, can we search by “why did it scale at 2:13 AM.”

[10:41] Markus Klein: Yes, in Console there’s a scaling history panel per pool. You can filter by time and it shows entries. Each entry includes desired replicas, applied replicas, clamp reason if any, and a short “explanation” field.

[10:58] Marta Klein: Explanation like free text.

[11:01] Markus Klein: It’s structured but rendered as a sentence. Underneath it’s reason codes plus the relevant numbers (queue depth, utilization).

[11:12] Priya Desai: Are these logs retained.

[11:15] Markus Klein: Standard retention is 30 days for scaling events, and longer with an enterprise retention add-on. Config changes are typically longer. We can confirm exact retention for your tier.

[11:30] Marta Klein: Okay.

[11:33] Markus Klein: I want to check if we’re aligned on naming: you might see “min_replicas/max_replicas” in some APIs. Sometimes people say “min_gpus.” The intent is the same: min and max serving units.

[11:49] Priya Desai: We’d prefer min/max GPU because we think in GPUs. But replicas is fine if it maps 1:1.

[11:56] Hyejin Park: For most Dedicated pools, one replica maps to one GPU worker, but there are cases with multi-GPU per replica depending on model size. In that case, max_replicas still maps to capacity units. We’ll be explicit in your pool config.

[12:14] Dylan Hart: So the max bound should be cost understandable.

[12:17] Markus Klein: Exactly. We can align the knob to “max GPUs” in the customer view even if internally it’s replicas.

[12:29] Evan Cho: Can we talk about pricing? Like if we set max=40, do we pay for 40 always.

[12:34] Markus Klein: In Dedicated reserved capacity, you pay for what’s reserved/committed, not what’s currently active. If you want pay-as-you-scale, that’s a different model, but most enterprise Dedicated is reserved for predictability.

[12:49] Evan Cho: Then why do we need autoscaling.

[12:52] Priya Desai: Latency and keeping the service stable without overprovisioning always-on. We still can reserve 40 but run at 20 if we can.

[13:00] Markus Klein: Right. Even if billing is committed, autoscaling matters for service health and operational simplicity, and for burst usage if you have a hybrid plan. For some customers, “max” is used more as a safety control to avoid accidental scale to the full reserve if not needed.

[13:17] Dylan Hart: Okay.

[13:18] Markus Klein: Also, some customers have a base commit plus burst capacity. In that scenario max is literally spend control.

[13:25] Evan Cho: That’s probably us eventually.

[13:28] Priya Desai: Now predictive. How do you do scheduled events. We have like a daily batch at 7am.

[13:35] Hyejin Park: There are a couple options. One is you provide a schedule, basically “cron style” expected demand, and we use that as a prior. Another is we learn patterns from history. The MVP is more on the learned side plus optional event calendar.

[13:53] Priya Desai: If the predictor goes wrong at night and it scales up, we’re spending more.

[13:58] Markus Klein: Two safeguards: confidence gating, and max. Also we can set a “predictive max step” so it can’t jump too far purely on forecast.

[14:10] Evan Cho: I like that. Can we see the confidence score in logs.

[14:13] Markus Klein: Yes, when forecast is used, confidence is included.

[14:20] Marta Klein: Is that considered customer data? Like are you training models on our traffic.

[14:26] Markus Klein: It’s telemetry used for capacity planning within your account. We’re not training a shared model on content. It’s aggregate request metrics (token counts, rates), not prompts. We can provide a data handling statement.

[14:44] Marta Klein: Good.

[14:46] Dylan Hart: Switching gears slightly — what happens when we hit max. Does it queue forever.

[14:53] Hyejin Park: There are a few layers. The router can throttle, you can get 429s, or you can queue with a max queue time. If queue time exceeds, we fail fast. The important thing is it’s controllable and observable.

[15:10] Priya Desai: We prefer fail fast with a clear error. Not like 30 seconds hanging.

[15:15] Hyejin Park: Yep, we can set max queue latency. And we also expose queue depth metrics.

[15:24] Markus Klein: One thing we recommend: if you set a hard max, you should define what your application does when throttled. Like fallback model, degrade features, etc.

[15:35] Dylan Hart: We can do that.

[15:37] Priya Desai: We might route some to Hosted as overflow.

[15:41] Markus Klein: We can talk about burst to Hosted as a policy. Some customers do that, but it’s a separate decision.

[15:48] Evan Cho: That complicates spend though.

[15:51] Dylan Hart: But it prevents outage.

[15:53] Markus Klein: Tradeoffs.

[15:56] Marta Klein: If you fail over to Hosted, is that audited.

[15:59] Markus Klein: Routing decisions are logged in observability but not necessarily in the same “scaling audit” view. We can make sure you have the right signals.

[16:11] Priya Desai: We’d want to limit that too. Like only overflow for internal assistant.

[16:17] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[16:20] Dylan Hart: Could you give an example of a scaling log entry. Like what fields.

[16:24] Markus Klein: Sure. Roughly: timestamp, pool_id, prior_replicas, desired_replicas, applied_replicas, min_bound, max_bound, clamp_reason (none/min/max), primary_reason (queue_depth, forecast, latency), and then a small set of numeric inputs like current token rate, queue depth, p95 latency.

[16:48] Dylan Hart: That’s perfect.

[16:49] Marta Klein: And config changes include actor.

[16:52] Markus Klein: Yes.

[16:54] Evan Cho: Can we get alerts when clamp happens. Like if it wants more but can’t.

[17:00] Hyejin Park: Yes, that’s a common alert: “clamped_to_max” rate above 0 for X minutes. It correlates with throttling risk.

[17:10] Priya Desai: Great. That’s what we need.

[17:14] Markus Klein: Quick check: timeline. When would you want to run a pilot.

[17:20] Dylan Hart: Ideally early December. We have budget this quarter.

[17:24] Markus Klein: Okay. We can probably do a sizing session next week and then set up a design partner pilot.

[17:33] Priya Desai: For the pilot we’d want like two regions, but we can start with one.

[17:38] Hyejin Park: Starting with one region is easier to validate the autoscaler behavior.

[17:42] Marta Klein: For security we need SSO and audit logs.

[17:46] Markus Klein: Dedicated includes SSO/SAML and RBAC, yes. Audit logs as discussed.

[17:54] Marta Klein: And encryption.

[17:56] Markus Klein: In transit and at rest, and for VPC deployments we support KMS integration depending on cloud.

[18:04] Priya Desai: Can we talk about “min during drains” again. It’s a bit scary.

[18:09] Hyejin Park: Totally. The honest answer is: if hardware is unavailable, we can’t conjure GPUs. But we’ll do everything to preserve min. And you’ll see it in logs as an availability event. Also you can request capacity reservation that makes min more reliable.

[18:28] Dylan Hart: We’re okay with that as long as max is strict.

[18:31] Evan Cho: And we get notified.

[18:33] Hyejin Park: Yes.

[18:35] Markus Klein: Another thing: some customers ask “can Redwood ever scale above max due to a bug.” The answer is the controller clamps, and we also have monitors that page us if we ever exceed. Bound violations should be zero.

[18:50] Marta Klein: That’s good. We’ll ask for that in the security questionnaire.

[18:55] Priya Desai: What about “cooldown” interacting with clamp. We’ve seen weird stuck behavior.

[19:01] Hyejin Park: Yeah, that can happen in naive systems. Our implementation treats clamp separately. Like if desired is below min we clamp to min, but we still track the underlying desired for the next loop so we don’t get stuck. There are guardrails.

[19:18] Priya Desai: Okay.

[19:20] Dylan Hart: How much control do we have over these knobs. Like is it a million settings.

[19:25] Markus Klein: We try to keep defaults sane. The primary knobs are min, max, and optionally cooldown. Advanced settings exist but we usually hide them unless needed.

[19:36] Evan Cho: I prefer fewer knobs.

[19:38] Priya Desai: I prefer more knobs (laughs).

[19:41] Markus Klein: We can keep it simple for the pilot.

[19:45] Marta Klein: For audit: do you log the advanced settings changes too.

[19:49] Markus Klein: Yes, any config change is logged.

[19:54] Dylan Hart: Okay. Next: what do you need from us.

[19:57] Markus Klein: Biggest thing is traffic shape. If you can provide token rate per minute over a week and note known events, we can propose min/max and whether predictive is worth turning on.

[20:12] Evan Cho: We can do that. Do you want it anonymized.

[20:15] Hyejin Park: Aggregate is fine.

[20:17] Priya Desai: We can share QPS and average tokens.

[20:21] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[20:24] Marta Klein: And for audit retention, can we get 90 days.

[20:28] Markus Klein: Likely yes for enterprise. We’ll confirm.

[20:33] Dylan Hart: Competitors wise, we’re also looking at Together and Bedrock. Bedrock doesn’t give us the knobs. Together is flexible but we’re not sure about audit logs.

[20:44] Markus Klein: Understood. Dedicated with strict bounds is a common differentiator.

[20:50] Priya Desai: Can you also send how “max” is enforced in the actual control loop. Like not marketing, but actually.

[20:56] Hyejin Park: We can send a technical note. High level: the policy engine evaluates your config and returns resolved min/max, then the autoscaler computes desired based on signals, then applies clamp. That clamp is in code and tested.

[21:12] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[21:14] Markus Klein: We probably don’t want to paste code in email, but we can give detail.

[21:18] Dylan Hart: Yeah.

[21:20] Marta Klein: Also, who can change max. Is it restricted by RBAC.

[21:24] Markus Klein: Yes. You can restrict autoscaling config changes to admin roles.

[21:29] Marta Klein: Good.

[21:31] Evan Cho: One more: if max is hit, do we still keep paying. Like if we burst to max and then back down, is there any overage.

[21:39] Markus Klein: Depends on contract structure. For pure reserved, no overage. For base+burst, usage above base may be billed, but max sets the ceiling for that as well.

[21:52] Evan Cho: We will want base+burst, probably.

[21:55] Markus Klein: Okay.

[21:57] Priya Desai: Sorry, I’m jumping: how do you compute “desired” from latency. Because latency is noisy.

[22:03] Hyejin Park: We don’t just chase p95. We use queue depth trends and throughput first, and latency is more like a guardrail indicator for overload. Otherwise you can oscillate.

[22:17] Priya Desai: That’s what we do too.

[22:20] Markus Klein: We also have oscillation detection metrics.

[22:23] Dylan Hart: Okay.

[22:25] Markus Klein: We’re at like half the call. Do you want to spend time on the audit log format and security details, or on pilot setup.

[22:33] Dylan Hart: Pilot.

[22:34] Marta Klein: I’m fine with pilot, but I’ll send the security questionnaire.

[22:38] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[22:40] Hyejin Park: For pilot, what model and hardware are you thinking.

[22:44] Priya Desai: We’re testing a 70B-ish model. Today on A100 80GB. We might move to H100.

[22:51] Hyejin Park: Okay. That influences ramp times and replica sizing.

[22:56] Priya Desai: Our peak is ~1.5k QPS, but tokens vary widely.

[23:02] Hyejin Park: That’s why we want token rate not just QPS.

[23:07] Evan Cho: I can export that.

[23:09] Markus Klein: Great.

[23:12] Dylan Hart: Also want to know: if we set max=40 and we accidentally have a loop where it tries to scale to 80, we need to see in logs “it wanted 80 but clamped.”

[23:23] Markus Klein: Yes, you’ll see desired vs applied.

[23:27] Marta Klein: And that can be used in postmortems.

[23:30] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[23:33] Priya Desai: One more question: If we reduce max, does it immediately scale down.

[23:38] Hyejin Park: Not necessarily immediately; it will be evaluated on the next loop. And if you set max below current, it will scale down to max, but respecting cooldown and safe drain behavior.

[23:51] Priya Desai: Okay.

[23:53] Evan Cho: That’s important: if I lower max because of spend, it should take effect quickly.

[23:58] Hyejin Park: It will take effect quickly, but we also have to avoid dropping live requests. So it’s “quickly but safely.”

[24:07] Markus Klein: And you’ll see that change in audit logs.

[24:11] Dylan Hart: Great.

[24:13] Markus Klein: Alright, maybe we do a quick recap and next steps, unless there are other blockers.

[24:19] Marta Klein: No, this was good.

[24:21] Priya Desai: I’d like that technical note.

[24:24] Evan Cho: And pricing structure around base+burst.

[24:28] Markus Klein: Got it.

[24:30] Markus Klein: Recap: you need strict max spend cap and predictable min floor. Max is enforced as a hard clamp. Min is enforced by the autoscaler, with exceptions for maintenance/capacity issues, which are logged. Scaling decisions are logged with reason codes and desired/applied, and config changes are separately audited with actor/time. Predictive pre-scale is optional and bounded by max, with confidence gating.

[24:56] Markus Klein: Next steps: we’ll send a one-pager on semantics and audit log fields, plus security materials. You’ll share traffic patterns and event schedule. Then we schedule a sizing/pilot scoping session next week.

[25:10] Dylan Hart: Sounds good.

[25:12] Priya Desai: Works.

[25:13] Evan Cho: Yep.

[25:14] Marta Klein: Great.

[25:16] Markus Klein: Cool. Thanks everyone.

[25:18] (call continues with a few minutes of scheduling logistics and calendar holds; transcription ends)
